localTips.title: Border and ferry logistics take time
localTips.description: Argentina–Chile crossings can be slow and some foods are restricted; keep passport handy and don’t pack fresh produce when crossing.

localTips.title: Connectivity is patchy—use offline tools
localTips.description: Download offline maps (Maps.me/Gaia) and keep cash for small towns; carry a power bank for long bus days.

foodToTry.title: Cordero patagónico (Patagonian lamb)
foodToTry.description: Order it “al palo” (spit-roasted) and reserve ahead at popular parrillas—it's often a limited daily run.

foodToTry.title: Centolla (king crab)
foodToTry.description: Best in Ushuaia/Punta Arenas; go for simple preparations (al natural/grilled) to taste the crab, and ask market price first.

foodToTry.title: Guanaco
foodToTry.description: Try it as stew or steak in Argentine Patagonia; it’s lean, so pair with a sauce and don’t order well-done.

foodToTry.title: Mate and facturas (or torta frita)
foodToTry.description: Grab bakery pastries for bus rides; in windy, cold towns, torta frita is a warm, cheap snack locals love.

gettingAround.title: Long-distance buses are the backbone
gettingAround.description: Book main routes (Calafate–Chaltén, Puerto Natales–Paine) early in high season; bring food and layers—heating can be inconsistent.

gettingAround.title: Rental car gives flexibility but plan for conditions
gettingAround.description: Expect gravel, strong crosswinds, and limited fuel; get full insurance, a real spare tire, and download offline routes.

gettingAround.title: In-park shuttles and catamarans save time
gettingAround.description: In Torres del Paine, coordinate shuttle times with your trek stages and confirm catamaran schedules the day before—they change with weather.

topThingsToDo.title: Erg dunes sunrise/sunset walk
topThingsToDo.description: Base yourself near Erg Chebbi (Merzouga) or Erg Chigaga (M’Hamid) and hike a dune ridge 30–45 minutes before sunrise for cool temps and fewer crowds.

topThingsToDo.title: Overnight desert bivouac (camp)
topThingsToDo.description: Choose a small camp away from the main dune “hotel strip” for quieter nights; confirm if toilets/showers are private and if the camp is on real dunes or hardpan.

topThingsToDo.title: 4x4 day route to remote landscapes
topThingsToDo.description: Book a half/full-day loop to visit desert plateaus, seasonal lake beds, and black-rock (hamada) terrain; insist on a fixed itinerary and fuel/meal inclusion.

topThingsToDo.title: Visit a desert oasis and khettara/irrigation sites
topThingsToDo.description: Stop at an oasis village to see date-palms and traditional water channels; go with a local guide to access farms respectfully and avoid getting lost in palmeraies.

topThingsToDo.title: Night sky stargazing away from lights
topThingsToDo.description: Ask your host to take you 2–5 km from camps/roads; bring a headlamp with red mode and download an offline sky map app before you leave coverage.

scamsToAvoid.title: “Mandatory local guide” ambush
scamsToAvoid.description: Some people claim you must hire them to enter dunes or villages; you don’t—use your pre-booked guide/driver or agree on a price beforehand if you choose one.

scamsToAvoid.title: Bait-and-switch camp upgrades
scamsToAvoid.description: Photos may show luxury tents but you’re placed in basic ones; get the camp name, exact tent type, and bathroom details in writing before paying a deposit.

scamsToAvoid.title: Inflated camel/quad add-ons on arrival
scamsToAvoid.description: Operators quote one price online then add “fees” for scarves, water, parking, or fuel; confirm total cost, duration, and what’s included (water, guide, helmet) upfront.

localTips.title: Pick the right season and timing
localTips.description: Best comfort is Oct–Apr; in summer, do activities only at dawn/dusk and skip midday rides when heat and wind are brutal.

localTips.title: Pack for sand and temperature swings
localTips.description: Bring a buff/scarf, sealed eye drops, and a zip bag for phone/camera; nights can be near-freezing in winter even after a hot day.

localTips.title: Choose Erg Chigaga for solitude, Erg Chebbi for ease
localTips.description: Chebbi is easiest for short trips and amenities; Chigaga is wilder but requires longer 4x4 transfers—plan at least 2 nights.

localTips.title: Respect desert etiquette
localTips.description: Ask before photographing people, especially women; keep music low near camps and pack out all trash (including tissues) since wind spreads it fast.

foodToTry.title: Medfouna (Berber pizza)
foodToTry.description: A stuffed bread often baked in sand/embers; order it in towns like Rissani/Merzouga and ask for a mild version if you’re heat-sensitive.

foodToTry.title: Mechoui (slow-roasted lamb)
foodToTry.description: Best shared in local grills/market days; arrive early because popular stalls sell out by afternoon.

foodToTry.title: Tagine with prunes or apricots
foodToTry.description: A sweet-savory staple that travels well for desert days; request less sugar if you prefer a more savory profile.

foodToTry.title: Saharan mint tea with dates
foodToTry.description: Often served very sweet; ask for “moins sucré” and pair with fresh dates from oasis farms when in season.

gettingAround.title: Shared taxis (grand taxi) to desert gateways
gettingAround.description: Use them to reach hubs like Merzouga, M’Hamid, or Douz; prices drop when the car fills—confirm fare per seat before boarding.

gettingAround.title: Private 4x4 with local driver
gettingAround.description: Best for remote dunes and off-road tracks; agree on exact route, stops, and return time, and make sure the driver carries recovery gear and extra water.

gettingAround.title: Camel transfer for short dune access
gettingAround.description: Ideal for a sunset ride to camp, not long-distance travel; ask for padding/blankets and a slower pace if you’re not used to riding.

topThingsToDo.title: Great Migration game drives (time it by region)
topThingsToDo.description: Dec–Mar: Southern Serengeti (Ndutu) calving; Jun–Jul: Western Corridor (Grumeti) crossings; Aug–Oct: Northern Serengeti (Mara River) crossings—stay 3+ nights in one area to avoid long drives.

topThingsToDo.title: Sunrise safari in the Seronera Valley
topThingsToDo.description: Leave the lodge at first light for big-cat action along the Seronera River; ask your driver to work known kopjes and shaded river bends for leopards.

topThingsToDo.title: Hot-air balloon over the plains
topThingsToDo.description: Book early and go on day 2–3 (weather buffer); pack a warm layer for pre-dawn and request a flight area that matches the migration’s current location.

topThingsToDo.title: Kopjes and rock art around Moru
topThingsToDo.description: Visit Moru Kopjes for lions on the rocks and ancient Maasai rock paintings; go mid-morning when cats start using the kopjes for shade.

topThingsToDo.title: Ngorongoro Crater day trip (logistics-aware)
topThingsToDo.description: If you’re based near Naabi Hill/Seronera, start before dawn and pre-arrange crater permits and lunch boxes; it’s a long day, so skip if you’ll lose peak Serengeti sightings.

scamsToAvoid.title: Unlicensed guides/vehicles offering “cheap Serengeti permits”
scamsToAvoid.description: Only enter with a registered operator or official park guide—ask for TALA/TTB registration and confirm park fees are paid at the gate, not “on the road.”

scamsToAvoid.title: Overpriced Maasai “village visits” with surprise add-ons
scamsToAvoid.description: Agree on total cost, duration, and what’s included (donation, photos, crafts) before you stop; pay one person, not multiple collectors.

scamsToAvoid.title: Fake park-ranger fines and checkpoint payments
scamsToAvoid.description: Rangers don’t collect cash roadside—any official payment is receipted at gates/offices; if pressured, ask to return to the nearest gate warden.

localTips.title: Choose camps by season, not by brand
localTips.description: A well-placed mobile camp can beat a luxury lodge that’s far from wildlife; match your camp to the migration’s current sector and your target species.

localTips.title: Carry small bills and tip discretely
localTips.description: Bring USD (post-2009 notes) or TZS for tipping and small purchases; tip guides and camp staff separately to avoid “shared” confusion.

localTips.title: Beat the radio-traffic at sightings
localTips.description: Ask your driver to arrive early, stay patient, and prioritize behavior over crowds; sometimes moving 500–800 m away yields better action and photos.

localTips.title: Pack for dust, cold mornings, and power gaps
localTips.description: Bring a buff/dust cover, warm layer for dawn, and a power bank; many camps run generators on set hours and dust can clog camera gear fast.

foodToTry.title: Nyama choma
foodToTry.description: Grilled meat (often goat or beef) served with chili and sides; best when done fresh at lodges that offer a BBQ night—ask for it “well done” if you prefer.

foodToTry.title: Ugali with sukuma wiki
foodToTry.description: Maize staple with sautéed greens; a filling, classic combo that shows up on staff menus—ask your camp if they can serve it for lunch.

foodToTry.title: Mishkaki
foodToTry.description: Spiced meat skewers; if you’re transiting through Arusha/Karatu, grab them at reputable spots where they’re cooked hot and fast.

foodToTry.title: Chai ya tangawizi
foodToTry.description: Ginger tea that’s perfect for chilly game-drive mornings; request it in a thermos for the vehicle if your operator allows.

gettingAround.title: 4x4 with a knowledgeable driver-guide
gettingAround.description: The Serengeti is best by private/vehicle safari—confirm a pop-up roof, radio etiquette, and that your guide knows seasonal road conditions.

gettingAround.title: Fly-in between regions to save time
gettingAround.description: Use light aircraft to Seronera, Kogatende (North), or Grumeti (West) to avoid full-day drives; pack soft bags and keep weight limits in mind.

gettingAround.title: Self-drive realities
gettingAround.description: Only consider with solid 4x4 experience, offline maps, and two spares; after rains, black-cotton soil can trap vehicles quickly—avoid isolated tracks.

topThingsToDo.title: Day trip to North Seymour (wildlife packed)
topThingsToDo.description: Go early for blue-footed boobies, frigatebirds, and sea lions; choose a small-group boat and confirm the landing time to beat crowds.

topThingsToDo.title: Snorkel Kicker Rock (San Cristobal)
topThingsToDo.description: Book a morning slot for clearer water; expect turtles, rays, and reef sharks—bring your own well-fitting mask if possible.

topThingsToDo.title: Walk Tortuga Bay + snorkel in the calm cove (Santa Cruz)
topThingsToDo.description: Arrive before 8:30am to avoid heat and get marine iguanas and sea turtles with fewer people; take water since there are no vendors.

topThingsToDo.title: Los Tuneles (Isabela) for snorkeling and lava scenery
topThingsToDo.description: Pick a tour that includes both snorkeling and the short lava walk; conditions are calmer than open-water sites and great for beginners.

topThingsToDo.title: Bartolome for iconic viewpoints and penguin chances
topThingsToDo.description: Choose a tour with a long snorkeling window at Sullivan Bay; bring reef-safe sunscreen and a light windbreaker for the panga ride.

scamsToAvoid.title: Unlicensed “last-minute” tours at the pier
scamsToAvoid.description: Only book with licensed agencies and ask to see the boat permit and what’s included (park guide, wetsuit, equipment, lunch) to avoid surprise add-ons.

scamsToAvoid.title: Overpriced taxi quotes outside ports/airports
scamsToAvoid.description: Confirm the fare before getting in and ask your hotel for the current fixed rates; in towns, short hops should be consistent and quick.

scamsToAvoid.title: Gear “damage fees” for snorkel/wetsuit rentals
scamsToAvoid.description: Inspect and photograph equipment on pickup and return; choose shops that provide a written checklist to avoid being blamed for old tears.

localTips.title: Bring cash and small bills
localTips.description: ATMs can run out, especially on Isabela; keep $1–$20 bills for water taxis, tips, and small restaurants.

localTips.title: Time your wildlife for tides and mornings
localTips.description: Ask guides about tide timing—snorkeling visibility and current strength change a lot; mornings are typically calmer with more animal activity.

localTips.title: Book inter-island ferries and flights with buffer time
localTips.description: Seas can be rough and schedules shift; avoid same-day tight connections and pack motion-sickness meds even if you “usually don’t need them.”

localTips.title: Pack a dry bag and reef-safe essentials
localTips.description: Panga rides are splashy and phones get soaked; bring a small dry bag, quick-dry towel, and reef-safe sunscreen (and apply after you’re out of the water).

foodToTry.title: Ceviche de camarón (shrimp ceviche)
foodToTry.description: Look for it at lunchtime menus; it’s fresher and cheaper midday than dinner spots near the docks.

foodToTry.title: Encocado de pescado
foodToTry.description: Fish stewed in coconut sauce—ask what the catch of the day is and request it “sin mucho aceite” if you prefer lighter.

foodToTry.title: Langosta (Galapagos spiny lobster, in season)
foodToTry.description: Order grilled with garlic butter; confirm it’s local and ask the price by weight before it’s cooked.

foodToTry.title: Bolón de verde + fresh juice (breakfast)
foodToTry.description: A filling plantain ball often with cheese or pork; pair with maracuyá or guanábana juice at local bakeries for a cheap early start.

gettingAround.title: Inter-island ferries (Santa Cruz–Isabela/San Cristobal)
gettingAround.description: Buy tickets from reputable agencies and sit toward the back for a steadier ride; bring a light jacket and keep valuables in a dry bag.

gettingAround.title: Water taxis at ports
gettingAround.description: Have small cash ready and confirm the per-person rate; ask which dock you’ll return to so you don’t end up far from your hotel.

gettingAround.title: Bikes and walking for town areas
gettingAround.description: Santa Cruz and Isabela are easy on foot or by bike; start earlier to avoid midday sun and carry water because shade can be limited.

topThingsToDo.title: Sunrise at Angkor Wat (with a smart spot)
topThingsToDo.description: Arrive 4:45–5:00am with your pass; skip the main reflection-pool crush by walking to the far-left pond edge for clearer views and faster exit.

topThingsToDo.title: Bayon at first light (crowd-free faces)
topThingsToDo.description: Go straight to Bayon after sunrise; climb the upper terrace early for the iconic stone faces before tour buses hit around 9:00am.

topThingsToDo.title: Ta Prohm when groups leave
topThingsToDo.description: Visit 12:30–2:00pm for emptier tree-root corridors; use shaded side paths behind the main gates for quieter photos.

topThingsToDo.title: Preah Khan + Neak Pean loop by bike or tuk-tuk
topThingsToDo.description: Combine these in the late afternoon; Preah Khan’s long halls glow in soft light and Neak Pean is a quick, peaceful detour if water levels allow.

topThingsToDo.title: Banteay Srei (best carvings) early with a stop en route
topThingsToDo.description: Leave Siem Reap by 7:00am to beat heat and crowds; pair it with a quick stop at a roadside palm sugar or lotus farm for a break from temples.

scamsToAvoid.title: "Temple is closed" or "special ceremony today" redirects
scamsToAvoid.description: Angkor sites rarely “close” unexpectedly; ignore anyone steering you to a different temple or shop and head to the official entrance yourself.

scamsToAvoid.title: Unofficial guide/monk bracelet or incense donation pressure
scamsToAvoid.description: If someone starts a “blessing” and asks for money, politely step away; only donate at clearly marked boxes if you choose.

scamsToAvoid.title: Tuk-tuk "cheap tour" that includes mandatory shops
scamsToAvoid.description: Agree on an itinerary and price (and no shop stops) before you depart; if they push shops, end the ride and pay only for time used.

localTips.title: Buy your pass the evening before
localTips.description: Get the Angkor Pass at the official ticket office after ~5:00pm to save dawn time; confirm your photo is clear and keep the pass accessible for checkpoints.

localTips.title: Use the small/quiet entrances
localTips.description: For Angkor Wat, enter via the side gates once inside the moat; for Ta Prohm, use less-used east-side paths to avoid bottlenecks.

localTips.title: Plan around heat and light
localTips.description: Do open, exposed temples early; save tree-covered Ta Prohm/Preah Khan for midday and return for golden hour at Srah Srang or Phnom Bakheng area (if access is open).

localTips.title: Respect dress and steep stairs
localTips.description: Cover shoulders and knees or you may be turned back; wear grippy shoes—upper levels have very steep steps, especially after rain.

foodToTry.title: Fish amok
foodToTry.description: Try the steamed curry in banana leaf; it’s best at Khmer-focused kitchens in Siem Reap rather than tourist buffet shows.

foodToTry.title: Beef lok lak
foodToTry.description: Order it medium with lime-pepper dip; ask for extra sauce and a side of rice if you’ve been temple-walking all day.

foodToTry.title: Nom banh chok (Khmer noodles)
foodToTry.description: Go early morning at local markets for the freshest green curry broth; add banana blossom and herbs for crunch.

foodToTry.title: Palm sugar sweets or fresh coconut
foodToTry.description: Buy from roadside stands on the way to Banteay Srei; check it’s sealed/clean and pay small notes to avoid “no change” hassles.

gettingAround.title: Hire a tuk-tuk with a fixed route
gettingAround.description: Set a day price and temple loop (Small Circuit/Grand Circuit) before starting; ask them to meet you at specific gates to save walking time.

gettingAround.title: Car/van for far temples and midday AC
gettingAround.description: Use a car for Banteay Srei or rainy season; it’s safer on slippery roads and lets you reset during the hottest hours.

gettingAround.title: E-bike or bicycle (only if you start early)
gettingAround.description: E-bikes are ideal for the Small Circuit with a dawn start; carry water, a power bank, and lock up at designated areas near entrances.

topThingsToDo.title: Old Faithful + Upper Geyser Basin (sunrise)
topThingsToDo.description: Arrive before 8am for parking and to watch multiple eruptions back-to-back; check the prediction board and walk the boardwalk loop while you wait.

topThingsToDo.title: Grand Prismatic Spring (best viewpoint)
topThingsToDo.description: Skip the crowded boardwalk photos and hike to the Grand Prismatic Overlook via Fairy Falls trailhead for the classic aerial view; go late morning for stronger steam-free color.

topThingsToDo.title: Lamar Valley wildlife drive
topThingsToDo.description: Be on the road at dawn or dusk for wolves, bison, and pronghorn; pull fully off the pavement and bring binoculars to avoid getting stuck in a “bear jam.”

topThingsToDo.title: Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone
topThingsToDo.description: Do both viewpoints: Artist Point for Lower Falls and Brink of Upper Falls for power; start at South Rim early, then cross to North Rim before midday crowds.

topThingsToDo.title: Mammoth Hot Springs terraces + historic Fort Yellowstone
topThingsToDo.description: Walk the Lower Terraces at golden hour when colors pop, then drive the Upper Terrace loop; add the short self-guided stroll around the old fort buildings.

scamsToAvoid.title: “Guaranteed” wildlife tours or “wolf sightings” promises
scamsToAvoid.description: No one can guarantee wolves or bears; book operators who refund/discount on no-show days or who focus on skills (tracking, optics) rather than promises.

scamsToAvoid.title: Overpriced roadside “park pass” help
scamsToAvoid.description: You only buy passes at official entrance stations or Recreation.gov for certain campgrounds; ignore anyone offering to sell or “upgrade” your pass outside gates.

scamsToAvoid.title: Fake hot springs “safe spots” or off-boardwalk shortcuts
scamsToAvoid.description: Anyone telling you it’s safe to step off trails is steering you into lethal ground; stay on boardwalks and report unsafe guiding to rangers.

localTips.title: Fuel and food run out faster than you expect
localTips.description: Top off whenever you see a pump (Canyon, Fishing Bridge, Old Faithful, Mammoth, Tower); groceries and quick meals sell out after mid-afternoon.

localTips.title: Plan around traffic “jams” and road delays
localTips.description: Build 30–60 minutes of buffer for bison crossings and construction; keep a flexible loop plan and do popular stops before 9am or after 5pm.

localTips.title: Cell service is spotty—download maps and geyser info
localTips.description: Save offline maps and screenshot geyser predictions before entering; use the visitor centers for latest closures and eruption estimates.

localTips.title: Watch wildlife from far away (and stay legal)
localTips.description: Carry binoculars and keep at least 100 yards from bears/wolves and 25 yards from other wildlife; rangers ticket people who approach bison for photos.

foodToTry.title: Huckleberry ice cream or shake
foodToTry.description: A regional classic—grab it in gateway towns like West Yellowstone or Gardiner where portions are bigger and lines move faster than in-park.

foodToTry.title: Bison burger (local ranch, not novelty)
foodToTry.description: Look for clearly sourced Montana/Wyoming bison; ask for medium to keep it juicy since bison is lean.

foodToTry.title: Trout (where it’s locally sourced)
foodToTry.description: Order it in restaurants that specify source and preparation; avoid vague “trout” listings that are often imported farmed fish.

foodToTry.title: Hearty elk or bison chili
foodToTry.description: Great after long hikes and cool evenings; gateway-town diners often do better versions than grab-and-go in the park.

gettingAround.title: Drive your own car (best flexibility)
gettingAround.description: Start early and do a “one major area per day” plan (Geyser Basins, Canyon, Lamar/Tower, Mammoth); distances look short but roads are slow.

gettingAround.title: Use pullouts correctly
gettingAround.description: When you stop, get all four tires off the roadway and don’t block turnouts; if a line forms behind you, move on to keep traffic flowing.

gettingAround.title: Know seasonal road openings and shortcuts
gettingAround.description: Some roads close in winter and shoulder seasons; check the morning road report and use the Norris–Canyon/Tower corridors to pivot when loops get congested.
